runs.text: Price discrimination charges different prices for reasons beyond cost differences. It requires market power, information about willingness to pay (WTP), and limits on resale. Perfect first-degree discrimination charges each buyer their WTP; it can expand output to the efficient quantity and transfer consumer surplus to the seller.

transcript.sourceText: A theater charges students $8 and other adults $14 for the same seat. The policy can persist only if students cannot resell discounted tickets to adults; otherwise arbitrage would erase the price difference. Verification separates the groups, and the different prices reflect different demand elasticities.
